paper_title: MolLean: A Process-Verifiable Language for Chemical Reasoning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Chemical chain-of-thought can contain hallucinated structural and property claims. We thereby introduce MolLean, a process-verifiable language that grounds chemical reasoning in an explicit molecular state. A layered Lean-based kernel checks state transitions and assertions over molecular readouts, from primitive graph edits to compound transformations. Meanwhile, a typed witness protocol separates native structural checks from externally supplied measurements. We further introduce MolLean-MCP, a stateful tool interface that exposes these transitions, checks, and readouts during generation: the model receives feedback to decide its next action, and rejected actions leave the state unchanged. MolLean supports one-pass trace execution, whole-trace refinement, and interactive reasoning through MolLean-MCP. We evaluate these three modes with direct chain-of-thought on 8,800 matched examples across 12 tasks spanning molecular generation, editing, optimization, and reactions. With Qwen3.6-27B, whole-trace refinement outperforms direct chain-of-thought on all 12 tasks. MolLean-MCP complements whole-trace refinement with stepwise verification feedback, reaching better performance in reaction tasks. Together, these results highlight an executable foundation for chemical reasoning, in which explicit chemical commitments can be checked and revised rather than remaining solely in free-form explanations.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Chain-of-thought prompting makes models intermediate reasoning visible (Wei et al., 2022). In chemistry, this is appealing as chemists could examine the intermediate reasoning steps to improve the explainability of the final answer (Wang et al., 2026; Narayanan et al., 2026; Li et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2025). However, model can invoke functional group absent from molecule, lose track of bond, or claim property improvement without establishing it. Analyses of chemical reasoning find fabricated structural claims even alongside correct answers (Li et al., 2026b), and broader evaluations reveal uneven chemical competence and overconfidence (Mirza et al., 2025). These errors concern the stated chemistry itself, failure mode complementary to causal unfaithfulness, where an explanation misrepresents how the answer was produced (Turpin et al., 2023). We therefore ask what must chemical reasoning language represent for its steps to be verifiable? Lean offers precedent: model proposes derivation and proof assistant checks its formal obligations (Moura & Ullrich, 2021; Jiang et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2023). Chemical reasoning combines graph transformations, structural observations, empirical estimates, and choices among plausible candidates. Chemistry tools already support capable agents (M. Bran et al., 2024; Boiko et al., 2023); the key step is to give successive operations and claims shared molecular referent and an explicit acceptance condition. We introduce MolLean, process-verifiable language grounded in maintained molecular state (Figure 1). transition constructs, modifies, or reorganizes represented molecules. readout obtains information without changing them, and an assertion tests claim against that information. The state does more than record the output: it determines which atoms later edit addresses, which molecule property readout measures, and whether an accepted prefix remains usable after failed proposal. MolLean supports primitive edits, construction macros, joint transformations, and candidate introduction at different granularities. An accepted edit supplies the referent for subsequent checks, and rejected edit leaves the maintained state intact. Verification thus applies directly to the models declared commitments. We expose the same language through whole-trace and interactive interfaces. MolLean One-pass submits complete trace; MolLean Refinement revises rejected trace from the initial state. MolLean-MCP lets the model inspect the current state, attempt an operation, and use immediate feedback to choose its next action. External feedback is central to revision: tool-grounded criticism guides reasoning more reliably than intrinsic self-correction (Huang et al., 2024; Gou et al., 2024). MolLean specifies what that feedback refers to and when it commits change. Our contributions are as follows: state-grounded chemical reasoning language and verification contract. MolLean unifies molecular transitions, readouts, and assertions, with explicit boundaries between native structural checks and externally witnessed claims. Two feedback regimes over shared execution semantics. Whole-trace refinement revises complete traces from the input; MolLean-MCP interacts with the maintained state and commits only accepted edits. An evaluation on 8,800 matched examples across 12 tasks. With Qwen3.6-27B, refinement improves over direct chain-of-thought on every task, and MCP reaches the highest reaction accuracy. On ChEBI-20, refined traces reach 79.0% soundness and 33.1% answer accuracy, identifying task fidelity as the next challenge beyond repairing rejected steps. Qwen3-4B gains substantially on structural tasks.

sections.title: 2 MolLean
sections.content: MolLean is reasoning language built around simple contract: an operation refers to the current molecular state, verification decides whether it is admissible, and only an accepted transition commits new state. Readouts and assertions observe that same state without editing it. Lean implements the chemical core, while Python handles parsing, state transport, reference resolution, and inference control (Figure 1).

sections.title: 2.1 A Language Grounded in Molecular State
sections.content: Execution begins at S0 = init(x) for task input x. The state contains active molecules, leaving pool, atom references, and bookkeeping counters. Molecules are graphs labelled with elements, bonds, charges, radicals, and aromaticity. The leaving pool retains fragments that are excluded from the answer and tracked in bookkeeping. Generation can start empty; other tasks load the supplied molecules. transition attempts to change the state. readout observes it without changing its molecular contents, and an assertion constrains that readout, for example by requiring count or property improvement. Complete traces express these constraints; the interactive interface also exposes valuereturning queries. Edits form one class of transitions, alongside construction, candidate introduction, and fragment separation. Let at be declared operation, Γ the verifier configuration, and the external provider. sections.title: 2.2 State Transitions at Different Granularities
sections.content: Seven primitives add or remove atoms, form or break bonds, and update bond order, charge, or radicals. They check preconditions and affected valences. Intermediates may be under-saturated to permit construction, and connectivity is enforced by the relevant operation or terminal policy. Construction macros such as Chain, Ring, and AttachGroup reduce index manipulation. Compound actions express joint bond changes, proton transfer, and fragment separation. Fragment splits bridge bond into active molecules; Eject moves separated component into the leaving pool. Named reactions expand into these operations. Most expansions execute in Lean; Python fragment adapters submit operations for the same checks. Granularity determines the verification unit. Concerted bundle applies edits atomically and checks the resulting valences once all edits apply. propose introduces structurally checked candidate in single step. Bookkeeping covers graph atoms, formal charge, and radical parity across both pools. Addition, removal, and candidate introduction update the ledger accordingly. Charge and radical balance are closing obligations. Terminal realizability checks valence, connectivity, aromaticity, and closed-shell rules.

sections.title: 2.3 State Readouts and External Witnesses
sections.content: A readout associates query with the state being examined. MolLean supports native checks for seven structural families: atom counts, bond counts, ring counts, molecular formula, aromaticity, built-in functional-group patterns, and retained R/S stereocenter annotations. Element counts include implicit as well as explicit hydrogen, while molecular-formula checks require all present elements. Ring counts use graph-theoretic definition.

sections.title: 2.5 Whole-Trace and Interactive Inference
sections.content: MolLean One-pass executes generated complete trace until acceptance or the first rejection. MolLean Refinement starts from that same completion, returning rejection feedback and indexed state to the model. It revises rejected traces within fixed budget, restarting each at S0 and stopping once accepted. Thus the model can replace its entire plan after failure. MolLean-MCP exposes transitions, checks, and readouts as stateful tools, supplied to the model as function-calling schemas within the inference loop. The model can inspect the state before choosing its next operation; rejected proposals leave it unchanged. finish invokes closing gates. MCP uses the language interactively; One-pass and Refinement submit complete programs. Verification compares only against the input or self-proposed candidate; dataset references enter only the independent scorer (Section 3). Each task declares its initialization, allowed operations, closing obligations, and scorer.

sections.title: 3.1 Tasks, Protocols, and Metrics
sections.content: All protocols are evaluated on the same 8,800 examples across 12 task types: 500 examples for each of nine S2-Bench tasks (Li et al., 2026a), 500 forward and 500 retrosynthesis examples from USPTO-50k (Schneider et al., 2016), and the complete 3,300-example ChEBI-20 test set (Edwards et al., 2021; 2022). Reaction classes are supplied to every protocol, and USPTO uses deterministic reaction-level split. Invalid answers and unsuccessful episodes remain in the denominator. Protocols. Direct CoT generates free-form reasoning and final SMILES answer. MolLean One-pass emits one complete trace without feedback. MolLean Refinement starts from the same one-pass completion and allows up to eight whole-trace refinements. MolLean-MCP constructs trace through stateful tools, with up to two attempts and 30 counted calls per attempt. We abbreviate these protocols as CoT, One-pass, Refine, and MCP. All MolLean results use the same verifier version; Appendix D.2 details the inference settings. Metrics. S2-Bench generation and editing use structural-count and functional-group-change success criteria. sections.title: 3.2 Whole-Trace Refinement Improves Task Performance
sections.content: Refinement improves over Direct CoT on all 12 task types  (Table 1)  , with gains of 12.048.2 percentage points under each tasks binary success criterion. For optimization, this range uses direction-only success, and similarity-weighted scores show the same gains. Atom and bond counts improve by 46.8 and 48.2 points, and component addition by 44.2. Paired bootstrap intervals for the primary Refine-minus-CoT score exclude zero in every task  (Table 2)  . One-pass already improves over CoT on 11 tasks. On forward reactions, One-pass (23.6%) trails CoT (35.0%), and refinement raises accuracy to 62.8%, showing that feedback is most valuable when the initial plan misses the verifiers obligations. Improvements extend to reference-based tasks, with ChEBI-20 accuracy increasing from 18.1% to 33.1% and retrosynthesis from 3.0% to 20.8%. sections.title: 3.5 Whole-Trace Inference with Qwen3-4B
sections.content: The smaller-model evaluation shows substantial gains on several structural tasks  (Table 3)  . It uses the same task IDs and whole-trace protocols as the main evaluation. Relative to Direct CoT, refinement raises atom-count success from 15.8% to 56.8%, component addition from 13.4% to 91.4%, substitution from 15.2% to 53.4%, and the logP optimization score from 14.7 to 60.0. Verification-guided refinement therefore transfers to smaller model. Reference-based generation remains difficult for the smaller model: after refinement, forward-reaction accuracy is 1.6% (One-pass: 2.2%), ChEBI-20 reaches 1.4%, and retrosynthesis is 0.0% under every protocol. These tasks depend on chemical knowledge that the proposer must supply, so verification is most effective when paired with capable candidate generator.

sections.title: 4 Case Studies: Repairs and Specification Gaps
sections.content: Figure 4 pairs molecular structures with verification feedback in six cases, illustrating how rejected commitments are repaired and how an accepted revision can still miss the intended task. Valence and attachment sites. In the forward-reaction example (a), forming bond to an acyl carbon before breaking its bond to chlorine would give carbon valence five. The one-pass trace is rejected. Refinement replaces the sequential edits with joint bond-formation and bond-cleavage operation, removes the detached chlorine, and obtains the correct carbonate product. The aldehydeaddition example (c) instead needs different attachment site: the same AttachGroup macro fails at substituted aromatic carbon 10 and succeeds at carbon 11. The revised trace then passes the functional-group-change and input-relative similarity checks. The carbonate requires suitable action granularity, whereas the aldehyde requires suitable molecular referent. Measured properties and explicit counts. In (b), the one-pass edits lower QED (Bickerton et al., 2012) from 0.674 to 0.573 despite an instruction to increase it. The graph edits pass, and the property assertion fails. Refinement reaches QED 0.767, with success-weighted similarity 0.743. RDKit supplies the measurement and Lean checks the requested direction. In (e), valid 27-carbon chain fails AtomCount because the instruction requests 25. Refinement proposes 25-carbon chain and passes that count. Both cases separate candidate validity from the requested property, with different evidence sources: atom count is native to the graph, and QED is an externally computed descriptor checked through witness.

sections.title: 5 Related Work
sections.content: Chemical language research connects molecular representations with natural-language descriptions and instructions. Text2Mol introduced text-based molecular retrieval and ChEBI-20 (Edwards et al., 2021); MolT5 studied translation between molecular and natural-language representations (Edwards et al., 2022); and Speak-to-Structure evaluates instruction-driven generation, editing, and optimization (Li et al., 2026a). SELFIES addresses molecular-string validity (Krenn et al., 2020), whereas structural reasoning targets molecular understanding (Jang et al., 2025). ChemBench evaluates chemical knowledge and reasoning more broadly (Mirza et al., 2025). These perspectives complement evidence that fluent chemical reasoning can contain unreliable structural claims (Li et al.,

sections.title: Preprint

Formal and executable reasoning make different parts of derivation checkable. Lean separates proof construction from proof checking (Moura & Ullrich, 2021); Draft, Sketch, and Prove links informal planning to formal proofs (Jiang et al., 2023), and LeanDojo supports programmatic interaction with Lean (Yang et al., 2023). Learned process supervision evaluates intermediate reasoning with trained verifier (Lightman et al., 2024). PAL and Program of Thoughts use execution to ground generated computations (Gao et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023). Feedback and tool use turn evaluation into part of generation. Self-Refine uses model-generated feedback (Madaan et al., 2023), and CRITIC grounds revision in external tools (Gou et al., 2024), which is more reliable than intrinsic self-correction on reasoning tasks (Huang et al., 2024). ReAct interleaves reasoning and actions (Yao et al., 2023). In chemistry, ChemCrow integrates specialized tools (M. Bran et al., 2024), Coscientist connects planning with experimental automation (Boiko et al., 2023), and ChemReasoner steers catalyst search using computational-chemistry feedback (Sprueill et al., 2024).

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: MolLean grounds chemical reasoning in maintained molecular state, combining Lean-checked obligations with explicit external witnesses. MolLean-MCP makes this feedback available during generation. Whole-trace refinement improves Qwen3.6-27B performance across all 12 tasks, MCP delivers the strongest reaction results, and Qwen3-4B gains substantially on structural tasks. Grounding instructions in explicit constraints is the natural next step toward chemical reasoning that is both verifiable and faithful to the task.

sections.title: A Implementation Details
sections.content: MolLean combines Lean checks with Python orchestration and external evidence providers. Table 4 distinguishes their responsibilities. Table 4: Verification components and execution semantics. Component Implemented check Execution semantics Molecule validator Native assertions Edits and bundles Bookkeeping External witnesses Python orchestration Proved valence and connectivity soundness; conditional aromaticity Graph predicates; six assertion-boundary theorems Preconditions, valences, bundle outcomes Atoms, charge, radical parity across both pools Typed request and predicate on returned fields Parsing, reference translation, serialization, control flow Validation of represented molecular graphs Checks on explicitly stated obligations Atomic validation of concerted bundles outcome Additions and removals update the ledger Provider and witness binding trusted State transport and inference control The validators validate sound theorem concerns the returned proof-carrying molecular object. Native assertion-boundary proofs cover AtomCount, BondCount, RingCount, HasAromatic, FGCount, and FormulaMatch. Hydrogen counts include graph and implicit hydrogens. Formula matching covers every present element and rejects duplicate element entries, while bookkeeping tracks literal graph atoms. A.1 Represented State and Reference Resolution The runtime serializes MultiMolState between Python and persistent Lean process. Its core fields are reproduced below; each TaggedMol pairs molecule identifier with graph. Listing 1: Core Lean state declaration (comments omitted). structure MultiMolState where : List TaggedMol active : List TaggedMol leaving_pool : Nat step_count : Nat init_atom_count init_charge : Int init_radical_parity : Nat structure AtomRef where mol_id atom_idx : AtomIdx : MolId molecular graph stores indexed atoms, bonds, and stereochemical annotations. Atom fields include element, formal charge, radicals, aromaticity, and virtual hydrogen information; bond fields specify endpoints and order. Virtual hydrogens contribute to element and formula readouts, and the bookkeeping ledger counts graph atoms. The leaving pool is excluded from the predicted answer and remains part of that ledger. Additions, removals, and proposals update the atom-count ledger. References are pairs (mol id, atom idx) into the graph state. cross-molecule bond joins two index spaces, and fragment split creates new molecule identifier. In whole-trace execution, Python tracks accepted primitive merges and remaps subsequent step references through that history. Lean separately rebases references inside tracked compound bundles. MCP uses the current atom map returned in feedback for later model calls. Python also exports the maintained graphs to molecular strings.

sections.content: A.2 Action Dispatch and Commit Semantics Complete traces are JSON objects with trace array. step identifies an operation family, for example op with primitive, macro with construction macro, compound with joint transformation, or assert with claim. SMILES proposals are parsed into graphs before validation. MCP functions translate to these same step representations and run on the same chemical kernel. Listing 2 summarizes the dispatch path. Lean returns either an accepted state or structured error. The runtime replaces the maintained state only after acceptance. failed operation can therefore report an attempted edit without adding it to the accepted trace. Native assertions and external comparisons inspect the molecular graph without changing it. Listing 2: Stateful dispatch and the external-evidence boundary (pseudocode). action = translate(model_call, current_state) action = discard_model_supplied_witness(action) reply = lean.apply_action(current_state, action) if reply.need_witness: witness = provider.answer(reply.request, initial_input) reply = lean.apply_action(current_state, action.with_witness(witness)) if reply.accept: current_state = reply.state record_accepted_action(action) return current_state_and_indices(current_state) else: return rejection_and_unchanged_state(reply.error, current_state) Primitive edits validate their preconditions and affected valences. concerted bundle validates its joint outcome, which accommodates edits whose sequential ordering would pass through temporarily over-valent graph. The closing procedure checks charge and radical bookkeeping and the tasks terminal obligations. Realizability and single-output requirements are task dependent (Appendix D). A.3 Concrete Typed Witness Native functional-group checks use Leans built-in patterns. pattern without native definition requests an RDKit fg count witness, whose returned count Lean compares with the assertion. Native StereoCenterCount counts retained R/S annotations. Bonding changes at tracked center conservatively remove its annotation. For native AtomCount, Lean counts the represented atoms of the requested element, includIn contrast, ing the applicable hydrogen convention; no provider-supplied count is needed. PropertyChange(qed) requests an RDKit measurement. The provider evaluates the current molecule and the bound initial input, then supplies integer-valued fields. Lean requires computable=1 and compares out x1000 with in x1000 in the requested direction. Listing 3 is the actual accepted payload from the QED case in Appendix C.2. Its values encode an increase from approximately 0.674 to 0.767. Lean checks the predicate on these returned typed fields. Listing 3: Accepted QED assertion and its supplied witness. sections.title: D Evaluation Details
sections.content: D.1 Task Setup and Scoring Generation begins from an empty state; editing and optimization begin from the input molecule. Forward prediction begins from reactants and retrosynthesis from the product. Editing requires one active output molecule and disallows whole-molecule replacement, while optimization permits candidate proposals. Generation, ChEBI-20, and reaction tasks use terminal realizability checks. Closing bookkeeping applies throughout. Non-reaction tasks score the first active molecule; reactions score the full active set. rejected whole-trace completion can still provide scored answer from its available state, or parsed answer when no state is returned. Failed certification can therefore coexist with correct answer. Missing or invalid answers receive zero. Selected episodes ending in context exhaustion are no-results, remain in the denominator, and receive zero score and certification; CoT and One-pass answers for the same example are scored independently. ChEBI-20 uses its full supplied test split. USPTO selection uses MD5(reaction key) mod 100 90, with key combining patent identifier and row index. Forward and reverse versions of reaction remain on the same side. We evaluate 500 examples per direction and supply reaction class names to all protocols. Optimization direction success is reported below separately from the similarityweighted main-table score. Table 6: Qwen3.6-27B optimization direction success (%).
